title: Attacking the Kingside! | GM Naroditsky's Top Theory Speedrun | Owen's Defense

moves.spoken: Against Owen's b6 we start with d4 — an incredibly effective system that drains the fun out of this offbeat opening.

Nc3 defends e4 naturally, and here's the first fork: the lazy Nf3 sleepwalks into trouble, because Black's whole idea is Bb4, pinning the knight and piling onto the e4-pawn until careless players simply drop it.
moves.teaches: Against ...b6/...Bb4 setups, don't develop on autopilot — the target is the e4 pawn behind the pin.

moves.spoken: The antidote is Bd3, shoring up e4 before the pin can bite.
moves.teaches: Pre-reinforce the pawn the coming pin will attack.

moves.spoken: After Bb4 comes the crux — Ne2, not a3. It connects the knights, so Bxc3 loses its sting and the b4-bishop is neutered, and we never have to weaken ourselves with f3.
moves.teaches: Ne2 defuses a ...Bb4 pin by connecting the knights, without the concession a3 or f3 would make.

moves.spoken: Best of all, we escape the pin by simply castling — more flexible than a3, since the b4-bishop is harmless, and if Black trades on c3 himself we've saved the a3 tempo. Look how compact this is: e4 is solid, e5 is ready, and the bishop on d3 already eyes h7 — the kingside attack is crystallizing.
moves.teaches: You can often step out of a pin by castling instead of spending a pawn move to break it.

moves.spoken: Bxc3 is a positional mistake — handing over the bishop pair for nothing. Now a Bg5 pin bites hard, because there's no dark bishop left to answer it with Be7.
moves.teaches: Giving up the bishop pair unprovoked leaves you unable to neutralize the pins it used to cover.

moves.spoken: Black defends alertly with h6, so we amend the plan — and here we choose the principled, ambitious line rather than a quiet developing move.
e5 looks positionally wrong — it opens the long diagonal and hands Black a knight square on d5 — but its whole worth is tied to the attack that follows.
moves.teaches: A positionally 'bad' pawn push can be strong when it's the first move of a concrete attack.

moves.spoken: The point: with Black's dark-squared bishop gone, the dark squares and g7 are chronically weak, so the queen swings to g4 to hammer g7 — the same motif you see in the French Winawer, where an early ...Bxc3 leaves exactly these holes.
moves.teaches: When the enemy dark bishop is gone, attack the weakened dark squares around g7 with Qg4.

moves.spoken: Black can't castle into Bxh6, and g5 only helps us — that pawn is kindling. Open the f-file with f4 and the kingside catches fire.
moves.teaches: An enemy g5 pawn is fuel: pry the f-file open against it rather than fearing it.

moves.spoken: Even the endgame after Qxg5 is fine — we win a pawn and gain the f-file with pressure on f7 — but the middlegame attack is what we're really after.
The g5-pawn becomes a battering ram: g6 is a huge threat, tearing open the shelter in front of the king.
moves.plans: Ram g6 to smash the kingside pawn cover.

moves.spoken: Black's d6 ignores the real threat, so we press on — there are still plenty of pieces to attack with, and the win is there even in an endgame.
g6 is the intuitive hammer — open the f-file and cash in on Black's undeveloped queenside while it lasts.
After recapturing with Bxg6-check the whole kingside caves in.
Rf7-check drops the rook onto the seventh rank, skewering everything and feeding the attack — a move that simply cannot be bad, so play it without agonizing.
moves.teaches: A rook check that lands on the seventh rank is almost always right — take it on principle.

moves.spoken: Now hunt for mate, but don't get tunnel vision: this is a danger zone where players obsess over checkmate and forget that just winning another pawn or piece wins the game.
moves.teaches: Look for mate, but never forfeit a simple material win chasing a prettier one.

moves.spoken: Follow the rules — start with a capture. exd6 forces the king to recapture, and the point is the follow-up.
moves.teaches: When in doubt, examine checks and captures first — the simplest forcing move is often best.

moves.spoken: Bf4-check develops the bishop with tempo and defends the rook at the same time, leading straight toward mate.
Be5 defends the d4-pawn with tempo and, crucially, strips the king of every escape square — and once the king has no squares, you start hunting mating nets.
moves.teaches: When the enemy king runs out of squares, switch from winning material to building a mating net.

moves.spoken: The elegant finish is a pawn mate: b3 threatening c4. Even Rxg6 fails, because Re1 removes the last escape square and mate follows — and to be certain of a sacrificial net like this, run through every single legal reply piece by piece; there are fewer than you'd think.
moves.teaches: Verify a forced mate by checking every legal enemy move; it's faster than it sounds and catches freak defenses.
